subject: Critical Thinking
title: A Brief History of Propaganda
description: A micro-lesson that makes A Brief History of Propaganda usable.

hook.text: The word 'propaganda' was coined by the Catholic Church in 1622 – to spread the faith. It wasn't a dirty word.

buildup.text: WWI governments discovered mass propaganda: posters, films, and newspapers could manufacture public opinion at scale.

discovery.text: Edward Bernays, Freud's nephew, turned propaganda into 'public relations' — same tools, new name, commercial purposes.

twist.text: Nazi Germany proved propaganda could make an entire nation complicit in genocide. Goebbels studied Bernays's work.

climax.text: Modern propaganda uses the same principles – repetition, emotion, us-vs-them – but at algorithmic speed & global scale.

punchline.text: Propaganda didn't disappear. It got an internet connection.

quiz.question: Who coined the concept of modern 'public relations' using propaganda techniques?

details.summary: Propaganda has existed since ancient empires used monumental architecture and inscriptions to project power. From Roman coins to World War posters to social media campaigns, the tools change but the playbook of emotional manipulation remains remarkably consistent.
details.whyItMatters: Recognizing propaganda patterns across history lets you spot the same techniques in modern advertising, politics, and social media before they influence your thinking.
takeaways: Propaganda predates modern media by thousands of years
The core techniques have changed far less than the technology
Historical awareness is the first defense against manipulation

faq.question: What are the oldest known examples of propaganda in history?
faq.answer: Ancient Egyptian pharaohs and Mesopotamian kings used monumental inscriptions and imagery to project divine authority. Roman emperors stamped their faces on coins distributed across the empire, a mass communication medium of its era.

faq.question: How did propaganda evolve with the invention of the printing press?
faq.answer: The printing press enabled mass-produced pamphlets and posters, turning propaganda from a tool of the elite into a weapon available to anyone who could write. Martin Luther's printed theses sparked the Reformation partly through propaganda techniques.
